correctness.rationale: Any fixed rim containing both the hub opinion and another has a forbidden adjacent interface, where a non-hub opinion is outvoted by two hub-colored neighbors. With no hub color on the rim, its only allowed alphabet is the other two opinions; a rim vertex changes exactly at a singleton run, and the hub remains its absent third opinion exactly when the two rim populations tie. This gives the all-length bijective classification. Marked run starts yield n/r times the square of a length-composition count. The independent four-state transfer has characteristic equation λ⁴−(1+z)λ³+zλ²−z², a primitive φ Perron root, mean half, variance (5+3√5)/40, and distinct weighted self-loops ruling out nontrivial Fourier resonances; these establish the claimed even-length local CLT. Direct enumeration n=3..11 and a separate transfer comparison n=4,6,..,80 passed. No experiment is used as infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The theorem classifies three-color wheel fixed states under an inertia-preserving tie rule and derives their exact parity-dependent count and asymptotic. This rule differs from pure Nash neighbor-coordination best response: a vertex may retain an incumbent with fewer neighbors than either of two tied leading opinions. The indexed binary wheel fixed-state and general coordination-game results therefore do not imply the three-color count. Literature search did not identify all-wheel three-opinion covering work; obscurer unindexed equivalent results remain possible.

source_inspections.title: Exact two-cycle census for synchronous majority on wheel graphs

value.rationale: Wheel graphs are a standard hub-and-cycle social-influence family. The finding establishes a qualitative and mathematically sharp behavior: odd-rim graphs have only three consensus equilibria while even-rim graphs have exponentially many nonconsensus equilibria with a completely unrepresented hub opinion, using one fixed local rule and the same graph construction. The all-length exact sum, two-color contrast, entropy φ, Gaussian correction and independently verifiable finite cases make a natural complete stationary-state classification beyond a routine small-graph census. No generic basin or convergence significance is asserted.
